memory_lessons.applicability: Use as context for testing a different work-per-thread mapping; these are individual measurements, not confirmation results.
memory_lessons.claim: The recorded 128-thread float2 trial measured 0.2882 ms, the 256-thread four-accumulator tail-handled trial 0.2940 ms, and the eight-accumulator trial 0.3389 ms. Increasing accumulator count alone did not improve these observed times.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Measure the 64-thread, four-contiguous-element mapping across required sizes and seeds, checking the FP64 error bound and full-call time.

proposal.hypothesis: The measured 128-thread float2 mapping is the current strongest T3 result, while the valid 8-accumulator variant was slower than the 4-accumulator trial. Test a contrasting mapping with 64-thread CTAs: each lane owns four contiguous values within the same 256-element tile and uses float4 loads only for aligned, complete tiles, with guarded scalar handling for unaligned inputs and tails. Keep 1024 CTAs/partials, tile boundaries, and the 256-thread finalizer fixed. Whether wider per-thread work improves full-call time while meeting the FP64 error bound remains for controller measurement.

retained: Use a fused absolute-sum first stage with 1024 CTAs and 1024 partials, followed by the existing one-CTA, 256-thread finalizer.
Keep each CTA's 256-element global tile boundary and grid-stride progression, but use 64 threads with four contiguous elements per lane.
Use float4 loads only when the input pointer is 16-byte aligned and the tile is complete; use guarded scalar loads for unaligned input and partial tails.
Reduce per-thread sums with CUB and overwrite every partial and the final output on each call.
